scenes.text: So, how do you build a strategy for your own community? Name the biggest health issue in the community you know best. Then answer three questions. How do you know it's the biggest, from data or from what people say? Who in the community is most affected? And what would you need to see in three years to say it had improved?

Start by working out the issues, using two sources, because each is blind to something. Local data compares the community with the state, splits it by group, and shows conditions, service use and the causes, like income, housing and transport. But it can't see why, or small groups that get averaged away. The community's own account sees the bus that stops at six, the building people won't enter, and what's been tried before and failed. But it misses slow trends, conditions people don't know they have, and issues nobody wants to raise. So use both. Where they disagree, that's a finding in itself. Then shortlist with three tests. How much harm does it cause? How unequally is it spread within the community? And can anything be changed at the level you can act? The second test often changes the priority.

Now build strategies, under all four goals. Take a regional town where type 2 diabetes is more common and starts earlier, mostly in its lowest-income areas. Under SDG 3: earlier testing in general practice, a continuing care plan, and removing cost barriers to medicines and foot and eye checks. Under SDG 4: food skills and health literacy through schools, reaching families through their children. Under SDG 10: aim at where the burden is, not the town average, and design it with residents of those areas. Under SDG 11: what local shops stock and charge, safe walking routes and lighting, and transport to services. Then advocacy, acting on decisions made by others. A town can do a lot itself, but it can't decide where the bus goes or what the state funds. So it puts the case to the council, the state government and local businesses. Improve what you can, and advocate for what you can't.

The syllabus asks how you know strategies may be effective, before they run. So it's about the reasoning, and your strategy checklist already holds most of it. Four lines you've used since Year 11. Does it act on the cause? If the problem is cost, education won't touch it. Will it reach the people carrying the burden? A better average can hide a wider gap. Will it last past the first funding cycle? And how would you know? Year 12 adds two lines. Is there a stated mechanism, step by step? Without one, it's just a hope. And has that mechanism worked elsewhere, allowing for what was local? Then sharpen how you'd know: a baseline, process measures for now, outcome measures for later, split by group. Match them to the lag time, the delay before health changes. Cheaper medicines can show up in months. School completion won't show in adult diabetes for twenty years. Judge that on a two-year health outcome, and you'll wrongly call it a failure.

Now be critical. Each line on the checklist has a matching failure. A strategy treats a symptom, not the cause, like healthy eating classes where fresh food is unaffordable and forty minutes away. It reaches the wrong people, because voluntary programs are taken up first by those already advantaged. It ends too soon, with two-year funding for a twenty-year problem. It's designed without the community, and nobody uses it. It measures nothing, or demands outcomes too early. And one failure isn't on the list yet. It depends on one person, so it stops when that person leaves. So before any strategy starts, ask one question. What would have to be true for this to fail? The answer tells you what to design against.

So here's the whole task in one structure. One, the issue, evidenced from data and the community, and who's most affected. Two, the causes, sorted by goal. Three, strategies under each goal, each with a mechanism, plus advocacy. Four, who it will reach. Five, how you'll know. Six, what could go wrong. Steps four to six are what most answers leave out, and they're what turns a list into an evaluation. And that's the idea this whole focus area kept returning to. Most of what decides a community's health isn't decided by its health services. That's why the goals are here, why advocacy sits beside improvement, and why the best plan usually includes something that doesn't look like health at all.
Two things to remember. Improve what you can, and advocate for what you can't. And ask how it could fail, before it starts.

Two exam questions. First. Proposal one: free sunscreen at the beach in a town with high skin cancer rates, to be judged after one year on melanoma deaths. Proposal two: a free after-school sport program at a club across town, with no bus. For each, name the effectiveness test it fails most clearly, and redesign it. Pause here to answer.

The sunscreen fails the measurement test. Melanoma deaths lag by decades, so one year will show nothing. Measure use and sunburn instead, and add shade. The sport program fails on reach. With no bus, the children who most need it can't get there. Run it at schools, or add transport. The classic mistake is judging the idea instead of testing it.

Second. In a community, childhood tooth decay is concentrated in one low-income housing estate. Propose one strategy under SDG 10 or SDG 11, and one advocacy action, and explain how you'd know they may be effective. Pause here to answer.

Under SDG 10, take free dental checks and fluoride varnish into the estate's school and childcare. For advocacy, push the state to fund public dental or water fluoridation. It may be effective because the mechanism is clear, it reaches the group carrying the burden, and you'd set a baseline and track checks and decay by area. The classic mistake is proposing without a mechanism.

So name the issue from two sources, fill every goal and the advocacy row, test the mechanism, reach and measures, and ask how it could fail. That completes health in an Australian and global context. Now the focus moves to the body in training. And it starts with a form. If exercise is good for almost everyone, why screen people before they start?
